## 1. Overview & Core Concepts

In ServiceNow, the Service Catalog acts as the digital storefront for end users to request services, equipment, access, or automated actions.

When a user submits a catalog item, ServiceNow processes the request using a 3-tier hierarchy. Understanding this structure is essential for designing forms, routing approvals, and assigning work tasks.

### 2. The 3-Tier Request Hierarchy

Every submission in the Service Catalog follows a parent-child structure:

[ Request (REQ) ]

│

└───> [ Requested Item (RITM) ]

│

├───> [ Catalog Task (SCTASK 1) ]

└───> [ Catalog Task (SCTASK 2) ]

### Breakdown of Hierarchy Levels

Request (REQ): The top-level shopping cart container. It tracks overall order details, overall cost, and who placed the order. A single REQ can contain multiple items.

Requested Item (RITM): Represents a specific product or service ordered within the cart (e.g., "Developer Laptop" or "VPN Access"). Each RITM runs its own fulfillment logic and workflow.

Catalog Task (SCTASK): The actual work unit assigned to a specific group or person to fulfill the item (e.g., "Configure Laptop Hardware" or "Grant AD Group Access").

## 3. Database Table Schema Reference

ServiceNow stores catalog configurations and transactional data in specific system tables.

### 4. End-to-End Fulfillment Lifecycle Flow

+-------------------+       +--------------------+       +---------------------+       +-------------------+

| 1. Form Submission| ----> | 2. REQ Generation  | ----> | 3. RITM Execution   | ----> | 4. SCTASK Work    |

| User submits item |       | Cart creates REQ   |       | Trigger Flow/Workflow|       | Fulfillers complete|

+-------------------+       +--------------------+       +---------------------+       +-------------------+

│

▼

+-------------------+

| 5. Item Closure   |

| RITM & REQ Close  |

+-------------------+

### Detailed Lifecycle Steps

Submission: The user selects an item, fills in variables, and submits the form via Service Portal or Now Mobile.

Order Generation: ServiceNow generates a sc_request record (REQ). High-level approvals (like manager approval for total spend) execute at this tier if configured.

Item Initialization: A sc_req_item (RITM) record is generated under the REQ. The assigned Flow Designer flow or workflow starts automatically.

Task Assignment: The flow creates one or more sc_task (SCTASK) records assigned to specific teams (e.g., IT Helpdesk, Network Admin).

Closure: Once all SCTASK records are marked Closed Complete, the flow updates the RITM state to Closed Complete. Once all RITMs under a REQ are complete, the REQ is automatically closed.

## 1. Overview & Objectives

Creating a catalog item in ServiceNow involves configuring core administrative fields, portal presentation settings, access controls, and attaching a fulfillment process.

Administrators and developers can create items using either the native Service Catalog Module or the Catalog Builder interface.

### 2. Step-by-Step Procedure to Create a Catalog Item

1.Navigate to Catalog Items Module:System Administrator or Catalog Admin role required.

In the Application Navigator, go to Service Catalog > Catalog Definitions > Maintain Items. Click the New button at the top of the list view.

### 2.Configure Core Information:Populate essential identification fields.

Fill in the Name, Catalog, and Category fields to define where the item will be located and what users will see.

### 3.Attach Process Engine:Define execution engine.

In the Process Engine tab, select the appropriate Flow (Flow Designer) or Workflow that will execute upon submission.

### 4.Configure Portal Presentation:Optimize for Service Portal view.

Upload an icon and desktop picture, set search keywords, and write a clear Short Description and Description.

### 5.Save and Test:Verify in Service Portal.

Click Submit or Right-Click Header > Save. Click Try It or open the item in Service Portal to test display rendering.

## 1. Overview & Objectives

A Variable Set is a modular collection of variables that can be created once and shared across multiple Catalog Items. This eliminates duplicate effort and enforces consistency across the Service Catalog.

ServiceNow offers two primary types of Variable Sets:

Single-Row Variable Sets (Standard): Organizes fields into reusable sections or containers (e.g., standard "Requester Information" block).

Multi-Row Variable Sets (MRVS): Displays as an interactive grid/table allowing users to add, edit, and remove multiple rows of structured dynamic data during a single request (e.g., ordering software licenses for 10 employees).

### 2. Comparison: Single-Row vs. Multi-Row Variable Sets

### 3. Creating & Configuring a Multi-Row Variable Set (MRVS)

### 1.Navigate to Variable Sets Module:Application Navigator navigation.

### Go to Service Catalog > Catalog Variables > Variable Sets and click New.

### 2.Choose Set Type:Select set classification.

### Select Multi-Row Variable Set from the selection dialog.

### 3.Define MRVS Core Properties:Set operational limits and names.

### Title: Visual header displayed on the form (e.g., Access Entitlements).

### Internal Name: Database name used in scripts (e.g., access_entitlements_mrvs).

### Max Rows: Optional numeric limit restricting maximum entries (e.g., 10).

### 4.Add Variables to the MRVS:Add individual inputs to the set.

Open the newly saved MRVS record. In the Variables related list, click New to define columns (e.g., System Name, Role, Access Expiration).

### 5.Associate Set to Items:Link to Catalog Items.

In the Included In related list, link the MRVS to all target Catalog Items where this grid should appear.

## 4. Understanding Data Lookup Rules

Catalog Data Lookup Rules allow automatic population of catalog variables based on combinations of input variables. They map directly to predefined decision matrices stored in lookup tables without using server-side scripts.

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

|                            Catalog Data Lookup Engine                             |

## 3. Deployment Lifecycle via Update Sets

All catalog items, variables, scripts, and UI policies developed in a non-production instance must be captured cleanly within an Update Set for migration.

### 1.Create and Select Update Set:Capture developer changes.

Navigate to System Update Sets > Current Update Set. Click New to create a fresh update set (e.g., STOR-10423_New_Developer_Laptop_Catalog_Item), set it to In Progress, and make it your current working update set.

### 2.Build and Configure Catalog Item:Ensure all components log to update set.

Create the catalog item, variables, variable sets, catalog client scripts, UI policies, and Flow Designer flows. (Note: Ensure Flow Designer flows are explicitly published so they register in the update set).

### 3.Complete the Update Set:Mark set ready for migration.

Navigate back to System Update Sets > Local Update Sets, open your update set record, change the State to Complete, and click Save.

4.Preview and Commit in Test/Production:Retrieve and preview in Target Instance.

In the target environment, navigate to Retrieved Update Sets, fetch the update set from the source instance, run Preview Update Set, resolve any configuration conflicts, and click Commit Update Set.

- **Customer Network**: hosts monitoring tools (SCOM, SolarWinds, SNMP, external).  
- **Event Ingestion**: monitoring tools send events to the Mix Server via REST APIs.  
- **Mix Server**: receives, processes, and forwards events to ServiceNow.  
- **ServiceNow Rusty API**: receives events, creates event records, and performs post‑operations on the Event Table.

- **Scheduled Jobs**:  
  - **Event Processing Job** – runs every 5 seconds to apply event rules and generate alerts.  
  - **Alert Processing Job** – evaluates business impact and triggers remediation workflows.  
- **Alert Console / Operator Workspace**: display service impact (critical, not critical, somewhat critical).  
- **Binding Routes**: define CI bindings and nodes for event routing.  
- **Historical Event Streaming**: events can be streamed over the past year.  
- **Schedule Table**: holds definitions for all scheduled jobs.

### Alert Resolution & Incident Management
- **Alert Lifecycle**:  
  - Triggered when thresholds (e.g., storage > 80 %) are breached.  
  - Alert cleared automatically if resolved within 5 minutes.  
  - Incident is created for the alert and auto‑closed when the alert clears.  
- **ServiceNow Automation**:  
  - Automatically creates and closes incidents for infrastructure device alerts.  
  - Service desk handles remediation; no manual intervention required for auto‑resolved alerts.

## [16:00] Event and Alert Management Overview

- **Alert lifecycle**  
  - Alerts are **auto‑resolved** after a configurable timeout (e.g., 5 minutes).  
  - Once cleared, the system **auto‑closes** the incident; no manual intervention is required.  
  - Service desk teams **do not** manage these auto‑closed incidents; they focus on unresolved alerts.

- **Incident creation**  
  - When an alert is generated, an **incident** is automatically created.  
  - The incident is linked to the corresponding alert and inherits its severity.

- **Event ingestion**  
  - Events are first **inserted into the event table**.  
  - A scheduled job processes events **every 5 seconds**.  
  - The job resolves the event to a CI ID via the EM register node table.

- **Alert generation**  
  - Based on the event’s severity, an alert is inserted into the **alert table** as **warning** or **critical**.  
  - Severity calculations are displayed in the **operator workspace**.

- **Operational workflow**  
  - Alerts appear in the **operator workspace** for monitoring.  
  - The system automatically handles alert‑to‑incident conversion and closure; remediation is performed by the relevant teams.

## [19:02] Operator Workspace Overview

- **Purpose**  
  - Provides a **global view** of services, including alerts, metrics, incidents, and road‑car analysis.  
  - Accessible from two locations:  
    - **Agent workspace**  
    - **Service operation workspace**

- **Data consistency**  
  - Both workspaces display the **same data set**; changes in one are reflected in the other.

- **User interaction**  
  - Users can **browse** alerts and incidents, view **severity** levels, and analyze **service health**.  
  - The workspace is designed for quick situational awareness and incident triage.

- **Key features**  
  - Real‑time alert visualization.  
  - Integration with metrics dashboards.  
  - Incident management tools (e.g., assignment, status updates).

- **Service dashboard integration**  
  - The operator workspace hosts the **service dashboard**, which aggregates CI and service data for quick reference.  
  - **CIs** (Configuration Items) such as LDAP, QA audit, production audit, and Windows servers are displayed and can be mapped to services.  
  - Users can view **service mapping** and understand how individual CIs contribute to overall service health.

- **Agent and service operation workspaces**  
  - **Agents** handle incidents, change requests, and service requests; they may need to inspect related CIs to diagnose issues.

## [43:42] Latency Issues in Event Processing
- **Latency** is the delay in network communication or response time.  
- Data packets traveling between points incur a measurable time delay.  
- Verify the **bucket field** in events to diagnose latency problems.  
- Avoid running applications more than twice to reduce potential latency (context unclear).  
- **Bucket field**:  
  - Value **>0** accelerates event processing by enabling multiple parallel jobs.  
  - Value **0** gives the job lower priority; it will not be scheduled at the front.  
  - Setting a higher bucket value increases priority and can reduce latency by allowing faster parallel execution.  
- Parallel jobs can introduce latency; balance bucket values to optimize performance.  
- **Event sources**:  
  - Third‑party system services, agent client collectors, connectors, SNMP, custom scripts, REST API inbound email actions.  
- **Real‑time event generation**:  
  - Can be configured via Dynatrace; manual event creation is possible for testing.  
- **Event retention & rotation**:  
  - Stable rotation groups determine how many days events remain in the system (e.g., 7, 5, 10 days).  
  - ECCQ events are subject to the same rotation; default buffer time is ~7 days out of the box.

## [48:03] Stable Rotation Groups & Event Cleanup

- **Stable Rotation Groups**  
  - Define how long events remain in the system before automatic cleanup.  
  - Typical retention periods shown: **7 days**, **5 days**, **10 days**.  
  - The number of days can be configured; after this period events are **removed** from the system.

- **Cleanup Process**  
  - Once the configured days elapse, events **disappear** from the system.  
  - This ensures the event store stays lean and only recent data is kept.

- **ECCQ (Event‑Cycle Control Queue)**  
  - Also governed by stable rotation settings.  
  - Default buffer time for ECCQ is **7 days** “out of the box”.  
  - ECCQ events are cleaned up after the same retention period.

- **Event Report Fields**  
  - When an event report is created, the system populates a set of predefined fields.  
  - Example field: *value* (placeholder) – the actual data that will be stored.  
  - Each field has a **description** explaining its purpose.  
  - Review the field list carefully; ask questions if anything is unclear.
